screeningScope: Full-text source, eligibility, study-design, taxonomy, and synthesis-readiness review of queue positions 1-12 after Batch 10 publication.

decisionDefinitions.INCLUDE: Eligible for evidence extraction and synthesis after full-text review.
decisionDefinitions.DEGRADED: A required source or verification element was unavailable.

records.sourceFile: Partially constrained group variable selection to adjust for complementary unit performance in American college football - 2024.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Using Football Bowl Subdivision data from 2009-2019, this application note combined natural splines, grouped penalties, and constrained optimization to adjust offense and defense ratings for schedule, home field, and complementary-unit performance. Non-scoring defensive turnovers were the most consistent positive complement to offensive scoring, but complementary adjustment did not materially outperform schedule and home-field adjustment in game prediction.
records.limitations: Team-season observational data contain reverse causality because score state and play calling alter within-game totals. Efficiency measures reduced but did not eliminate endogeneity, play-by-play sequencing was unavailable, and similar prediction error across adjusted approaches limits evidence of added operational value.
records.synthesisCaution: Use the method as an analytics example and hypothesis generator, not a player-health model or causal ranking of unit quality. Validate any derived team metric prospectively in the local decision process.

records.sourceFile: Positional comparison of countermovement jump performance in American collegiate football athletes.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Eighty-five Division I football players completed three force-platform countermovement jumps. Skill players had the highest jump height and modified reactive-strength index, linemen the greatest body mass and takeoff momentum, and linemen used longer braking, propulsive, and total takeoff durations than midskill and skill groups.
records.limitations: The single-program, male cross-sectional sample collapsed diverse positions into three groups. The study did not test longitudinal fatigue sensitivity, training response, football performance, injury, or the predictive validity of the proposed benchmarks.
records.synthesisCaution: Interpret jump strategy relative to position, body mass, and the athlete's own baseline. Cross-sectional group means are not universal talent standards or within-athlete fatigue thresholds.

records.sourceFile: Poor isometric neck extension strength as a risk factor for concussion in male professional Rugby Union players.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Neck strength was measured up to three times in 225 professional male rugby players during one season, in which 30 concussions occurred in 29 players. A 10% higher isometric extension value was associated with a 13% lower concussion rate after adjustment (IRR 0.87, 95% CI 0.78-0.98); no other direction or composite score was significant.
records.limitations: The observational association does not prove that strengthening prevents concussion. Only 74 players completed end-season testing, injury and international-duty absences may introduce selection bias, only 30 events supported the model, and results may not generalize to female, youth, amateur, or other-sport populations.
records.synthesisCaution: Neck extension training is a plausible component of collision preparation, not a substitute for technique, rule, exposure, equipment, recognition, or medical management. Do not treat the reported association as a protective threshold.

records.sourceFile: Position-specific kinanthropometric traits of professional American football players - A study of Mexican LFA players.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: ISAK-standard anthropometry in 189 Mexican professional players showed clear position-related size, composition, somatotype, and proportionality patterns. Linemen had the greatest absolute size and adipose, muscle, and bone mass; an exploratory three-variable discriminant model classified position with 57.7% accuracy.
records.limitations: The league-specific cross-sectional data were collected in 2019-2020, excluded kickers, used anthropometric fractionation rather than DXA or densitometry, and did not test performance outcomes. The exploratory classification model was not cross-validated and had only moderate accuracy.
records.synthesisCaution: Use these values as population-specific descriptive references, not body-composition targets, selection rules, or evidence that changing morphology will improve performance.

records.sourceFile: Previous injury is associated with heigthened countermovement jump force-time asymmetries in professional soccer players.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Seventeen previously severely injured and 17 uninjured professional male soccer players completed dual-force-platform countermovement jumps. Previously injured players had greater concentric and most eccentric force-time asymmetries despite no group difference in bilateral jump-performance outcomes.
records.limitations: The cross-sectional design cannot show that injury caused the asymmetry or that asymmetry predicts reinjury. The small sample pooled different lower-extremity injuries, lacked preinjury baselines, and could not identify the neuromuscular or structural source of the differences.
records.synthesisCaution: Inspect phase- and variable-specific bilateral kinetics when available, but do not use one asymmetry cutoff or normal jump height as a stand-alone return-to-sport decision.

records.sourceFile: Profile of cervical endurance and peak isometric strength in elite professional male rugby players.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: In 136 elite male rugby players, front-row forwards had the greatest isometric cervical strength and backs the lowest. Extension force was highest overall (429 ± 104 N), flexion lowest (275 ± 65 N), and only peak flexion strength related significantly to flexion endurance; position, age, body mass, and individual variability affected interpretation.
records.limitations: One preseason time point in a male professional cohort cannot establish seasonal stability, injury risk, or readiness thresholds. Prior training and some surgeries varied, criterion validity of the strength test was not established, test order was fixed, and endurance failure relied partly on visual judgment.
records.synthesisCaution: Use position-aware values as contextual norms and prioritize an athlete's repeatable baseline. They are not concussion-protection targets or return-to-contact cutoffs.

records.sourceFile: Factors Contributing to Chronic Ankle Instability- A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Systematic Reviews.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: An overview of 12 systematic reviews reanalyzed primary studies of ankle-instability factors. Dynamic balance, peroneal reaction time, and eversion-strength deficits had strong support and proprioception and static-balance deficits moderate support for nonspecific ankle instability, but only 17% of primary studies used a clearly defined chronic-ankle-instability population.
records.limitations: Eighty-three percent of primary studies failed recommended CAI criteria, prediction intervals were wide, outcomes and definitions were heterogeneous, and much of the evidence preceded consensus inclusion standards. Findings for nonspecific instability cannot be assumed to characterize well-defined CAI or prospectively predict recurrence.
records.synthesisCaution: Use a multidomain ankle assessment and rehabilitation plan, but do not label one balance, reaction-time, proprioception, or strength test as the cause of CAI or a clearance threshold.

records.sourceFile: Foam rolling training effects on range of motion - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Eleven controlled or randomized studies with 290 mostly young adults and 46 effects found a moderate range-of-motion benefit from repeated foam rolling (effect size 0.823, 95% CI 0.325-1.322). Effects were larger after more than four weeks and varied by muscle, with no ankle-dorsiflexion gain after triceps-surae rolling.
records.limitations: The main model had substantial heterogeneity (I2 72.76%) and one very large effect; populations, outcomes, dose, intensity, and frequency varied. Subgroups covered only three moderators, the sample was mainly young adults, and performance or clinical benefits were not established.
records.synthesisCaution: Foam rolling can be one tolerable route to a specific ROM goal. Do not assume every joint responds, that more than four weeks is a universal minimum, or that ROM change automatically improves performance or injury outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Got Beer - A Systematic Review of Beer and Exercise.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Sixteen studies of beer and exercise had a mean PEDro score of 5.1. Lower-alcohol beer retained fluid better than stronger beer under standardized intake, nonalcoholic polyphenol-rich beer had limited respiratory-illness evidence, and moderate intake showed no clear chronic body-composition or strength effect; results were mixed and context-dependent.
records.limitations: Most samples were small and male, exercise and hydration protocols lacked ecological validity, alcohol blinding is difficult, only two studies allowed ad-libitum recovery intake, and chronic studies lasted just four to ten weeks. Nonalcoholic-beer findings cannot be attributed to ethanol.
records.synthesisCaution: Do not position alcoholic beer as a recovery strategy. Prioritize water, electrolytes, carbohydrate, protein, sleep, safety, and team policy; distinguish nonalcoholic products from alcohol-containing beer.

records.sourceFile: Head, Face, and Neck Cooling for Performance - A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Sixty-three controlled studies with 618 participants, 86.6% male, tested 75 head, face, or neck cooling strategies. Pooled self-paced and fixed-intensity performance effects were compatible with no effect through moderate benefit, cooling improved local temperature and thermal perception, and heart-rate, core-temperature, and mean-skin-temperature effects were negligible.
records.limitations: Nearly all studies had some risk-of-bias concern, cognitive outcomes could not be pooled, women were underrepresented, and modalities, doses, environments, and tasks varied. Improved comfort without meaningful core-temperature reduction limits physiological inference.
records.synthesisCaution: Cooling can improve comfort and may aid performance, but perception must not replace heat-illness prevention, acclimation, hydration, environmental monitoring, and emergency procedures. Test only rule-compatible strategies.

records.sourceFile: Hydration, hyperthermia, glycogen, and recovery - Crucial factors in exercise performance - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Eighteen studies with 158 participants were reviewed and 13 meta-analyzed. Hydration versus remaining dehydrated did not produce a significant pooled glycogen effect and was highly heterogeneous, while four temperature studies showed lower postexercise glycogen with greater heat exposure. The authors concluded that hyperthermia and dehydration may interact to worsen glycogen use and restoration.
records.limitations: The quantitative evidence was small, often decades old, and rated fair or poor; hydration estimates spanned both directions with I2 91.88%. Heat and dehydration are tightly coupled, protocols and biopsy timing varied, and mechanistic glycogen outcomes do not directly quantify sport performance.
records.synthesisCaution: Control heat strain and restore fluid and carbohydrate according to measured losses and turnaround demands. Do not use this heterogeneous synthesis to prescribe one replacement volume or claim hydration alone guarantees glycogen recovery.

records.sourceFile: Intermittent Fasting - Does it affect sports performance - A systematic review.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: This systematic review summarized 25 athlete or exercising-adult studies of time-restricted eating, intermittent fasting, and Ramadan fasting. Most reported preserved strength and performance with possible fat-mass reduction and lean-mass maintenance, but Ramadan studies and selected aerobic tests showed adverse effects under sleep, fluid, and schedule disruption.
records.limitations: Fasting types, duration, caloric intake, sports, tests, and samples were highly heterogeneous; several studies did not quantify energy intake, many were short, and the review did not meta-analyze effects. Caloric deficit, adherence, sleep, hydration, and Ramadan-specific practices confound attribution to fasting windows.
records.synthesisCaution: Intermittent fasting is not inherently performance-enhancing. Individualize it with a sports dietitian around energy availability, protein, carbohydrate, hydration, sleep, training timing, health, and religious priorities.
